title: How the Mind Generates Reality
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Our brains create a mental framework that predicts what we'll experience based on past experiences and context, rather than directly perceiving reality. This means that our perception of the world is shaped by our brain's internal workings, including its history and assumptions, which can lead to misunderstandings and misinterpretations. By recognizing this, we can gain a deeper understanding of ourselves and others, leading to greater compassion, wisdom, and self-awareness.

sentences.text: I'm really appreciating the longer zazen period.
I hope that's not too hard on anybody.
It seems like a good thing, once a week, to have a little more room to stretch out into zazen.
I did notice a little discomfort in the body.
My body's pretty programmed for 30 minutes, but there's a lot more space for the mind to do what the mind does.
That's just on Wednesday night; all the other times we're sitting for 30 minutes.
So I hope that's helpful and not too challenging, or challenging in a good way if it is challenging.
Well, I want to continue this exploration of neuroscience and dharma.
A few more talks.
Oh, and by the way, next week we'll have a bodhisattva precept ceremony instead of a talk.
The intention is to do those on the first Wednesday of the month, and I actually forgot last week, which was my bad, but next week we'll remember and wait it.
Remind ourselves of the precepts and celebrate precept practice and focus on where we can work with precepts together.
Anyway, back to the brain.
We talked a little bit last week about this next section of seven and a half lessons about the brain, but my afternoon got rearranged by a vaccine opportunity.
So I wasn't able to prepare much last week, and I want to go back to it this week, because this bit of neuroscience is really what's most deeply affecting to me anyway.
I feel like it really strongly resonates with the Yogacara Buddhist teachings, as best I understand them, for understanding consciousness and how it all seems to work.

Although I do feel right away a little caution about that resonance between science and Buddhism, because I like for science and Buddhism to line up, and I for sure have a strong case of what the psychologists, the researchers, call confirmation bias.
I want my view to be confirmed, so it's easier to see evidence that science and Buddhism are lined up here and harder for me to see evidence that they might not be.
A bit of counterweight is that I've also done some studies around how they actually are quite different: very different worldviews, very different jobs that they're trying to solve.

Another book I'll recommend, but I don't think I'll run a lecture on it, is a great short collection of lectures by the Buddhist studies scholar Donald Lopez, called *The Scientific Buddha, His Short and Happy Life*.
He makes a really good case for the ways they are quite different.

He also looks into the history of religion, the 18th and 19th century especially, and how, as colonialism spread into Asia, Asian Buddhist leaders as well as Western sympathizers had some real reasons to want to make Buddhism look more scientific, so that it kind of survived the onslaught of Protestant missionaries and so on.

So there's a deep history behind this idea, and we've got to be a little careful that we don't, in some subtle fashion, map our Western view onto Buddhism, like another kind of colonialism, minimizing and diminishing what Buddhism might have to offer us if we just make it all tidy and understandable to us.
And that bias persists to this day, even in high circles, I think, at least to a certain extent.

You may know about the Mind and Life organization and project, where they get the Dalai Lama and other high Buddhist teachers, usually in the Tibetan tradition, together with prominent scientists to have dialogues.
I read another interesting little book about that; here's another reading recommendation.

The philosopher Evan Thompson has been involved in those dialogues, and he feels like they often skirt the issue and avoid a significant problem with the whole endeavor, much as he also appreciates everything about it.
So he wrote a nice little book called *Why I'm Not a Buddhist*, about this same topic: that Buddhism and science have some areas where they don't quite line up.
This idea of confirmation bias is actually a great pointer to what I find exciting about this section of the neuroscience book.
The brain isn't a neutral analytical engine that's responding in real time to what's happening out there.
Even in the very way we perceive things and understand things and understand self, there's a certain kind of confirmation bias, so to speak.
This idea that we're simply looking out at an objective reality and responding to what happens, she says, is pretty much an illusion that the brain creates for us.
The evidence is really strong that the brain is way more ahead of the curve than we think.
It's constantly making use of data, memories, past experiences from before.
And not just memories like we think of memories, like dreams and images and dialogues; the brain is privy to the whole physiological, psychophysical experience.
So the brain is also storing things like how your body was responding to whatever was going on.
If the brain remembers that the last time such and so happened, your heart was beating more quickly, that gives us some information that whatever that kind of thing is, it's probably important.
And the brain's ultimate intention, which is kind of personifying the brain, but what it's evolved to do, she says in the book, is to keep us going, right?
To keep us alive.
So the brain keeps track of things where we're more activated in a certain way and uses those past things to show us our supposed experience of the present.
This brings us back to the opening story of this chapter, which I did share last week, but it's really worth hearing again, even if you were here.
It's an amazing story, and it was featured in the New York Times article she wrote that turned me on to the book.
So here's the story.
*A few years ago, I received an email from a man who served in the Rhodesian army in southern Africa in the 1970s, right before the end of apartheid.
He'd been drafted against his will, handed a uniform and a rifle, in order to hunt down guerrilla fighters.
To make matters worse, before the draft, he'd been an advocate for the same guerrillas he was now required to treat as the enemy.
He was deep in the forest one morning, conducting practice exercises with his small squad of soldiers, when he detected movement ahead of him.
With a pounding heart, he saw a long line of guerrilla fighters dressed in camouflage carrying machine guns.
Instinctively, he raised his rifle, flipped off the safety catch, squinted down the barrel, and aimed at their leader, who was carrying an AK-47 assault rifle.
Suddenly, he felt his hand on his shoulder.
Don't shoot! whispered his buddy behind him.
It's just a boy.*
*He slowly lowered his rifle, looked again at the scene, and was astonished by what he now saw.
A boy, perhaps ten years old, leading a long line of cows.
And the dreaded AK-47?
It was a simple herding stick.
For years afterwards, this man struggled to understand this unsettling episode.
How could he have managed to [unclear: "miss see"] what was right in front of him, and nearly kill a child?
What was wrong with his brain?
As it turns out, nothing was wrong with his brain.
It was working exactly as it should have.*
So I think the one thing to really focus on about this story is that we are so conditioned to continue to believe that the eyes are like windows and the brain is looking out through them.
We believe that we really are always seeing things in real time and interpreting them, maybe.
Maybe sometimes we interpret things incorrectly and get a little confused.
Since we have that persistent belief, which this chapter is going to unwind, we could misunderstand this story and not get its full import.

We could think that it means the man's eyes did see cows, a boy, and a herding stick, but that he was so stressed out he mistook what he saw, that he mistook the cows and the herding stick for soldiers and AK-47s.
But no, what she's saying happened is that he actually saw soldiers and AK-47s the first time he looked.
That's what he saw, in detail.
Then luckily his friend interrupted him and he looked again, and this time he saw cows, a boy, and a herding stick.

The way she talks about it, and I looked up some of the references too, is that what we experience most of the time, maybe all of the time, I'm not sure about that, is actually a kind of controlled hallucination.
Our brains are not looking out through windows.
Our brains are in a dark, quiet place where they can't see or hear anything.
They're using sensory data, for sure, and that sensory data is accumulating over time.
But our brain's job is to keep us going, and so they have evolved to actually predict what we'll need to do next, using this stored information and contextual information.
And not just predict what we'll do, but predict what we'll see, what we'll experience.

So we are experiencing, in fact, what the brain thinks we should be experiencing, which is different from our usual framework of experiencing something in real time in an externally consistent objective world.
One of the neuroscientists she refers to in the notes has this quote:
*Our experience of the world comes from the inside out, not from the outside in.*
This is so radical.
What a transformation.
And what are its implications?
How deep does that go?
How deep does that go?
How much are we hallucinating the world?

And also, the information doesn't just make it in like we're taking pictures and seeing objects; everything that goes in for reuse and prediction is also interpreted radically by the brain to make meaning.
I think we know this, this is how we all think, even though we don't think about it because we do so much automatically.
If we look at a chair over there, you aren't seeing something that is essentially a chair.
The idea of chair is an invention, a concept.
You see lines and colors and shapes, and you know from past experiences this object, chair; you know what to do with it and everything.
Since you've encoded so much chair information, you don't have to think about this at all.
It's very fast, it's very automatic. [unclear: "pictures"] are good at chair recognition.
Even further, this predicting nature of the brain probably makes it such that when you see the desk, you actually are starting to see the chair before your eyes even take in those shapes this time.
You know there must be a chair there, and so you don't bonk into things or whatever.
We're sort of making it up when we try to give the brain reasons for stuff, but it really does seem like it works this way.
The brain is much more predicting what you're going to see than you seeing what you see.
And the brain's mostly right, so it works pretty well.
We get around pretty well, except when we don't, except when it's wrong.
But it gets even more weird than that, because the brain is not only making meaning of sensory objects, as if it clearly is seeing sensory objects and conceptualizing them into conceptual objects.
The brain is also using meaning and history and background to decide what the lines and objects and colors and shapes are, too.
So I've got an example for you.
Let's see if this works over the screen.
I'm going to do a screen share.
I'm getting high tech here.
It's a high tech [unclear: "dermatologist"].
You may have seen this puzzle before, but it's illustrative of this point.
Oops, wrong one.
Don't look at that.
Look at this.
I almost messed it up.
Here we have a checkerboard.
Can you see that okay?
Okay, thanks.
Here we have a checkerboard and a cylinder, and in the illustration the cylinder is casting a shadow.
There are two important squares to look at in this: square A up here and square B down here.
If your brain works like my brain, and apparently like every brain that has ever looked at this and recorded its observations, you may be seeing A as a dark gray square and B as a light gray square.
Is that the case?
Yeah, thanks for nodding.
There's a few people I can see.
When you're in screen share mode, I can't see very many people.
Well, check this out.
This is so strange.
It turns out that's wrong.
The brain is doing some meaning-based perception here.
They think, how can they really know, but they think that the brain is trying to compensate for the fact that there's a shadow on the one hand.
When a shadow goes across the middle of a red carpet, the carpet in the shadow is actually a different color than the rest of the carpet, right?
But you see it as all one red carpet with a shadow on it.
So the brain has this history with shadows, and it's trying to compensate for this shadow.
At the same time, the brain sees a checkerboard, and we all know what checkerboards are supposed to be like: alternating dark and light.
So here's the wild thing.
It turns out square A and square B are the exact same color.
Here's one illustration to show you that, and then I've got another way to show you.
In this illustration, they've taken a diagonal stripe, which is the color of A and B, and joined them together.
Isn't that weird?
Your brain is probably fighting right now.
Like, well, yes, no, yes, same, different, wait, what?
Okay.
See that?
Yeah, so we're seeing what isn't there.
We're seeing what the brain thinks should be there based on past history with shadows and checkerboards.
And actually, they're the same.
But here, watch this.
This is so convincing, and even more strange.
Where did I put it?
Oh, it's on the same share, darn.
Sorry.
It's the next part down.
These folks created a real live model of that illustration, with a real cylinder and lights and a big checkerboard, and she's going to show us what happens when we move the shapes back and forth.
Crazy, huh?
I'm glad I found that video because that really sends it.
It doesn't change colors when it moves, right?
Our brain is doing this meaning-based perception, perceiving based on context, and in the objective way we think of things, it's totally wrong.
Isn't that weird?
I'll send you guys the link to that if you want to keep tripping out on it.
Roll yourself a fat one and see what you can figure out.
So there's a lot going on here with our brains that we didn't know was going on with our brains.
And the question is, why does this really matter?

Well, I think it matters because the way we interact with ourself, the way we look at how we grow and change, the way we understand our patterns, the way we understand other people, the way we understand society, has a lot of assumptions baked into it from our simplistic misunderstanding of the brain.
And I think understanding this really has some implications for us, both for managing our own trajectory more wisely and for compassion, for understanding others, for wisdom and compassion.
Here's how she explains what happened with our soldier friend.
We'll go back to the book again.
Okay, she says:
*Now we can unravel why our soldier friend saw guerrilla fighters instead of a shepherd boy with cows.

His brain asked, Based on what I know about this war, and given that I am deep in the woods with my comrades gripping a rifle, heart pounding, and there are moving figures ahead, and maybe something pointy, I have no idea.*
I don't know.
*And the brain's result is guerrilla fighters.
In that situation, the stuff inside and outside the head didn't match, and the inside stuff prevailed.
Most of the time when you look at cows, you see cows.
But you've almost certainly had an experience like this soldier's, whether you knew it or not, where the information inside your head triumphs over the data that you've collected.
And the brain's result is guerrilla fighters.
Where the information inside your head triumphs over the data from the outside world.
Like have you ever looked at a friend's face in the crowd?
When you looked again, you realized it was a different person.
Have you ever felt your cell phone vibrate in your pocket* when it didn't?
Happens to me all the time.
*Have you ever had a song playing in your head you couldn't get rid of?
Neuroscientists like to say that your day-to-day experience is a carefully controlled hallucination, constrained by the world and your body, but ultimately constructed by your brain.
And in a very real sense, the predictions your brain makes are your brain having a conversation with itself.*
*A bunch of neurons make their best guess about what will happen in the immediate future based on whatever combination of past and present that your brain is currently conjuring.
Those neurons then announce that guess to neurons in other brain areas, changing their firing.
Meanwhile, the sense data from your world and your body injects itself into the conversation, confirming or not the prediction that you'll experience as your reality.
But in actuality, your brain's predictive process is not linear.
Usually your brain has several ways to deal with a given situation.
And it creates a flurry of predictions and estimates and probabilities for each one.
Is that rustling sound in the forest due to the wind, an animal, an enemy fighter, a shepherd?
Is that long brown shape a branch, a staff, or a rifle?*
*Ultimately, in each moment, some prediction is the winner.
And often it's the prediction that best matches the incoming sense data, but not always.
But either way, the winning prediction becomes your action and your sensory experience.*

So this has a lot of implications, she goes on to say, and I'm quite convinced by this, that when we're working with habitual responses to things, we're up against a different kind of challenge than we think we are.
When we habitually respond to something in, say, not such a great way, it's really hard, maybe almost impossible, for us to catch it and reverse the pattern or do something else.
And we get so frustrated, right?
Why did I do that again?
God, we get mad at ourselves.
One example I thought of is when I have to make a phone call.

Not other kinds of communication, but for some reason a phone call, when I think the person I'm calling is going to be annoyed or upset or there'll be a conflict, they won't want to hear what I have to say.
It's really powerful.
I very often freeze, feel nervous, feel afraid.
I notice a lot of procrastination, a lot of worry, a lot of rehearsing.
And the brain just seems to have such a strong association with this situation, and also the feeling that I have.
I feel heavy, I feel tense, I feel kind of hot, my cheeks grip in a certain way.
I shut down, often.
Next thing I know, I've convinced myself that this call really doesn't have to happen today.
Tomorrow will be just fine.

So I don't know, I guess the brain is predicting a difficult encounter that's going to drain my energy or something, trying to protect me from an expensive situation, mess up my energy budget, my allostasis, like she was saying earlier.
I don't know.
And of course I want to know why, but I'll probably never know why.
And yet, nine times out of ten, or maybe more, when I finally get my finger to hit the dot dang dial button on the phone, the conversation is just fine.
It's pleasant even.
And afterwards, freed maybe from that moment of fear of conflict, I feel really energized.
I feel really good, actually.
I feel better than I did before.
So I don't really know exactly what all the conditioning is.
I tell myself simple stories like "I'm conflict-averse," but what does that really mean?
There's something in there that causes this reactivity.
And I do have increasing respect for conditioning.
Conditioning is so powerful.

But the twist here, with the brain science that she's describing, and as we'll see it's much the same with Yogachara Buddhist understanding, is that once I'm already freezing up, it's pretty much too late for this time.
The brain has already created this fear-based reality, and I'm in it.
And the stress response is happening to some degree, and all the physiology is going on.
It's not just in my head, right?
My whole body is reactive and fearful.
Although it's not like I completely lose awareness of this.
Part of my conscious mind is able to think, well, maybe it won't be that bad.
Why are you so worried?
But the neural pathways and patterns are fired up, based on the past.
So I can't necessarily talk myself out of this.
In fact, so far I have been completely unable to talk myself out of this.
Eventually, I push through and have the positive experience again.
But then, here's the thing.
I could do the usual thing, which I now understand just makes it worse, which is to tell myself, "You, Ninny, silly me.
What were you so worried about?
That was nothing.
Next time, maybe you'll remember that these things aren't such a big deal."
Gah!
Which, in the Yogachara storehouse system, is just planting another kind of negative seed.
I was dumb.
I misunderstood.
I was overly subject to habit patterns.
And it's the same thing with the neuroscience.
That's reinforcing some kind of negative conditioning, and probably just makes it as likely or more likely that the next time I think of some call I'm worried about, it will be just as bad or worse.
But what the Yogachara storehouse consciousness with the seeds in it suggests, and what she suggests in the book, is that we can plant positive seeds instead, but we need to do that deliberately.
It's what she calls curating positive experiences.
And in Yogachara they say planting wholesome seeds.

So in that case, I realized, much better would be to really tune in to that good feeling I'm having when the call is going just fine after all, when I feel relieved and happy and energized at the end: to just revel in that, to feel into that, to encode that, and to feel it physically as well.
Because remember, the brain, and presumably the storehouse consciousness, is not just ideas, thoughts and memories.
It's your whole psychophysical state that's getting stored up and queued up for the next time around, when the brain has to predict what it needs you to do.
So just revel in the joy of it, and don't tell myself I should have done better, or I could have done this, or I should have known.
Because that probably just makes it worse.
So that's my hope.
I'm going to start on a program with this.
So if you want to have conflict with me, then I have to call you.
That would be great.
Let me know.
But isn't that interesting?
It doesn't seem like such a big change.
Both cases were about awareness, about noticing, and we talk constantly about being more aware and more accepting.
Geez.
So I'm going to instead focus on curating positive experience, planting positive seeds that we hope will germinate next time around, or the time after that, or the time after that.
But here's the thing also.
These systems require a lot of delayed gratification.

Because if we're deeply conditioned, or have a lot of negative seeds that are sprouting in that situation, and we can't even see inside the brain or inside the storehouse, we don't know how much is in there.
So we might not get a positive response.
I might take up this new plan, and the next time I have to make a scary phone call it's just as bad.
But what we can encourage ourselves with is this model, that naturally it takes a long time.
And we can be vigilant for when we respond to ourselves: what am I doing?
Am I adding positive or negative weight to this for the future?
Even though I probably can't solve it right now.
Because it already happened before it happened, right?
It's the strange thing about the brain predicting.
So we talk a lot about the present moment, which I'm feeling a little suspicious of.
How can we know what the present moment is if our brain is ahead of us?
So that's one aspect of all this.
But the other aspect is really maybe even more important, much as we all would like to get past all our foibles and be happy all the time.
To her credit, Dr.
Barrett makes a point about this in the book.
She does it pretty gently.
A really important part of the way we're conditioned to predict is through our biases.
And it's critically important that we learn about this so that we can have actual good relations and understanding across cultural groups.
It's not a matter of becoming colorblind, which is just a certain kind of denial, or of just noticing bits of negative prediction and trying to be better and set your intentions and get educated.
It's also about deliberately putting ourselves in situations where we can work through that process, deliberately or accidentally, and start to plant positive seeds, curate positive experiences.
Even though we're all well-meaning, and most of us probably consider ourselves in a certain kind of political and social orientation, and none of us is racist and all that, of course.
And yet, right?
And yet it's not just about our conscious ideas about who we are.
It's about our deeply conditioned selves, which happens even at a neurological, physical or mental basis, such that our mind is going to predict things, right?
And it's going to predict things that are wrong, just like the Rhodesian soldier, and it's going to predict things that we are convinced by at some level.
And it's so bad out there, right?

I was [unclear: "looking glass"] today at the New York Times homepage, and I saw a whole little cluster of different stories about different Black men being killed by white people and police for little or no reason.
It's so common, or maybe as common as it's always been but so much more reported, that it's like a department on the news: which Black men have been killed now.

And I think that learning about this stuff helps us to be more understanding, both of our own paths in anti-racism education and of others, and of the horrible things that happen, even as we oppose that horror.

Because the brains of these police officers, just like ours, probably really are predicting in a very convincing way that Black men are a threat, even though those predictions are largely or almost always wrong.
Like with the story of the soldier, the predicting is powerful because it's creating their reality.

So based on all this, I wasn't really that surprised by the woman police officer in the suburb of Minnesota, Brooklyn, whatever it's called, who shot Dante Wright with her revolver, thinking it was her taser.
Because if we think about it from this framework, it doesn't matter to us if a taser and a revolver look different and feel different and are different weights and different colors.
It sounds like the case was that her brain told her, I'm tasing this guy, and I bet in the split second before she pulled the trigger, she probably literally saw and felt a taser in her hand.
That's what her experience actually was, just like the Rhodesian soldier.
It's not like she mistook something; that's what she experienced, I assume.

And then, like in her opening story, where the soldier's friend tapping him on the shoulder caused a reassessment, caused a competing brain impression to win out, in her case it was the horrible report of the gun going off.
And she's reporting and saying something like, oh my God, I just shot him.
So it's horrible, it's totally horrible, but I think it's narrow-minded to be too surprised.
Another topic might be why heavily armed police officers are the ones asking people why their tabs have expired.
But that's something else.
So I think we should really keep studying all of this.
How do our minds really work?
From a neurological perspective, with this more recent neuroscience, and I read a bunch of her notes, I mean, what do I know really about neuroscientists?
I'm not a scientist, but it seems like it's all pretty convincing and the scientific community all agrees about this.
I watched a few TED Talks too.
Not really an expert, I watched a TED Talk.
And also reflect on how it does and doesn't match with whatever we are learning and have learned and will learn about Buddhist psychology.
Because here's where they really can work together.
The purpose of science is to understand reality in the most clear and objective way possible, although even science acknowledges that objective is a bit dubious.
But the purpose of Buddhism is [unclear: "salvage"], right?
The [unclear: "perfect"] of Buddhism is liberation, is reduction of suffering, is freedom.
And doesn't it seem like a lot of the suffering, or maybe all of the suffering, is from the way our minds are understanding reality?
Maybe if we understand our minds a little better, we'll understand reality in a way that's more healthy for us and for all beings.
I'll chant this out, and then maybe we can chat a little bit before we go.
*May our intention equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way. [unclear: "Beings are not allowed to save them."] Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it. [unclear: "Tell me about the Dharma Gates."] They're boundless, so be sure to enter them all.*
It's surprisingly harder to do these chants by yourself.
